questions.q: What is the actual scope of this capstone project?
options: Writing the product-catalog and checkout application code from scratch

Deploying and operating Northbridge's existing product-catalog and checkout container images on Kubernetes — Deployments, Services, Ingress, config, autoscaling, and packaging, not the app code itself
Designing a brand-new microservices architecture unrelated to anything built earlier in the course
Only writing a Helm chart, with no Kubernetes manifests or networking involved
questions.explain: The capstone takes existing container images and focuses on everything around them — placement, networking, configuration, scaling, and packaging — drawing on nearly every earlier chapter in the course.

questions.q: Why does the checkout service specifically get a HorizontalPodAutoscaler in this project's scope, while product-catalog's scope doesn't mention one?
options: HPAs can only ever be attached to one service per cluster
Checkout is described as having higher, spikier load (cart/order submission), which is exactly the traffic pattern autoscaling is meant to handle
product-catalog cannot be autoscaled because it is read-heavy
HPAs are required for every Deployment regardless of traffic pattern
questions.explain: The capstone scope ties specific pieces to specific real needs — checkout's spiky cart/checkout traffic is the textbook case for an HPA, while product-catalog's steadier read load doesn't demand the same treatment as urgently.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly listed as OUT of scope for the capstone?
options: Writing a Helm chart with environment-specific values files
Creating a ConfigMap and Secret for the checkout service
Wiring up a live, webhook-connected GitOps controller end to end against a real cluster
Setting resource requests and limits on each Deployment
questions.explain: The project requires writing an Argo CD Application manifest as a deliverable, but actually standing up a live GitOps controller with a working webhook is explicitly called out as optional, not required for 'done.'

questions.q: According to the 'what done looks like' checklist, which of the following is a required success criterion?
options: The cluster must be deployed to a specific named cloud provider
Both services' Pods reach Running and pass readiness checks, and helm upgrade followed by helm rollback both complete without error
The application code must be rewritten in a different programming language
At least five different Ingress controllers must be tested
questions.explain: The done checklist centers on operational correctness: Pods running and ready, a working Ingress route, a visible HPA with sane bounds, and Helm install/upgrade/rollback all functioning — not a specific cloud provider or rewriting the app.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize defining explicit in-scope and out-of-scope boundaries before any building begins?
options: Because Kubernetes requires a formal scope document before any YAML can be applied
Scope boundaries have no real purpose here beyond formality
To keep the capstone finishable and realistic to present in an interview, rather than open-ended or trying to cover unrelated extra work
Because the course forbids students from doing any extra work beyond the listed scope under any circumstances
questions.explain: A capstone with no defined boundary risks becoming unfinishable or unfocused. Stating what's deliberately excluded (e.g., live GitOps wiring, multi-cluster) keeps the project a concrete, completable, and defensible piece of portfolio work.
